title: Should I not have pity? (Jonah 4)
hook: God asks Jonah: should I not pity Nineveh, and much cattle too?
carry: doest thou well to be angry

segments.voice: Yesterday, Jonah prayed from inside the fish, and spoke of being heard before he was out. Your line was heard before he was out. Did you name a low moment from right where you were? Today, the end of Jonah's story, and it ends on a question. Day eight hundred twenty-six.

Jonah finally goes to Nineveh. He walks into the great city and cries out that it will be overthrown. And it works. The people believe. They fast and put on sackcloth, from the greatest to the least. The king comes down from his throne and sits in ashes. And God sees them turn from their evil way, and doesn't bring the disaster. A whole city spared. A prophet might be expected to rejoice. In the King James words: "But it displeased Jonah exceedingly, and he was very angry."
screen: `JONAH GOES TO NINEVEH.` → `THE CITY TURNS.` → `AND JONAH IS VERY ANGRY.`

segments.voice: Now we learn why he ran in the first place. Jonah tells God, in the King James words: "I knew that thou art a gracious God, and merciful, slow to anger, and of great kindness, and repentest thee of the evil." He quotes God's mercy back at God, as a complaint. He knew the city would be forgiven, and he didn't want it to be. God answers with a question: doest thou well to be angry? Jonah doesn't answer. He goes out east of the city, builds a little shelter, and sits to watch what will happen. And God makes a plant grow over him for shade, a kikayon, a gourd in the King James. Jonah is exceedingly glad of the gourd. The next dawn, a worm attacks it and it withers. A hot east wind blows, the sun beats on his head, and Jonah says he'd rather die. Then God speaks the last words of the book. "Thou hast had pity on the gourd, for the which thou hast not laboured, neither madest it grow; which came up in a night, and perished in a night:" And then: "And should not I spare Nineveh, that great city, wherein are more than sixscore thousand persons that cannot discern between their right hand and their left hand; and also much cattle?" The 1917 Jewish translation puts it: should not I have pity. And the book stops. We never hear Jonah's answer. The question is left hanging, for whoever reads it next. And the animals are in it too. God's pity reaches past people to the cattle of a foreign city. On Yom Kippur afternoon, Jews read this whole book, and the book ends right here.
screen: `GRACIOUS, MERCIFUL, SLOW TO ANGER.` · `A GOURD THAT GREW AND WITHERED.` · then, large: `SHOULD NOT I HAVE PITY ON NINEVEH?` · then: `THE BOOK ENDS ON A QUESTION.`

segments.voice: The practice: widen your mercy by one person. Breathe, and let your shoulders drop. Notice the people you find easy to wish well: family, friends, people like you. Then let your circle go out one step, the way Jonah's had to: toward a whole city. Think of one person from a place or group you'd rather not see spared. Someone from a city in the news, a rival team, the far side of an argument. Not someone who wronged you; just someone from the other side. You don't have to agree with them. Just hold God's question to Jonah, and let it be asked about them: should there be no pity here? If you pray, you can pray for their good. The bell holds the time.
kikayon, the plant God grew to shade Jonah, then let a worm destroy, the gourd of the King James. Today's word.

Your line: doest thou well to be angry. This week moved from Joel's dreams through Amos and Obadiah to Jonah's long way around. Today, when that place or group comes up, in the news or in talk, say one fair thing about the people in it. Day eight hundred twenty-six.

howItsDone: Jews read the whole book of Jonah at the afternoon service of Yom Kippur, ending with God's question about pity for Nineveh.

fork.setup: you're Jonah. the city you warned has turned and been spared. God asks, doest thou well to be angry? what do you do?
options: go out and sit east of the city, watching.
fork.reveal: Jonah doesn't answer. he sits outside the city to watch, and God teaches him with a gourd.

notes: Editor pass: review matches revised day-825 carry; 'enemy city' (not in the text) now 'foreign city'; practice and carry turned toward a place or group, as with Nineveh, so they no longer repeat day 823's rival/ex practice.
The JPS 1917 rendering 'should not I have pity' (Jonah 4:11) is mentioned without quotation marks; Keeper please verify the wording and whether to quote it.
Kikayon rendered gourd: KJV and JPS 1917 both have 'gourd'; the identity of the plant is uncertain.
Jonah as the Yom Kippur Minchah haftarah (with Micah 7:18–20 added in many communities) is stated simply; Keeper please confirm.

Audit 2026-10-01: practice said 'not someone who wronged you' then 'you don't have to excuse what they did'; contradiction fixed. Note: Jonah does answer God's second question (4:9); the script's 'Jonah doesn't answer' refers to 4:4 and stays accurate.
